summary:
Fire Watch is a web tool that merges NASA’s two active-fire satellite records, MODIS and VIIRS, into one harmonized fire record. Each satellite family sees fires differently, with different timing and resolution. The same fire can be counted twice, or a small early fire can be missed.

Our solution places both sensors on a common map and applies a simple rule. If both detect a fire, we count it once. If only one detects it, we keep it. The result is one combined fire map and one clean dataset. Users can pick any country or region, explore the combined map, and view an anomaly timeline that highlights unusual fire activity. We used Syria as our example region.

This directly addresses the challenge of harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS hot spots. We checked that the merged record keeps the trends, seasonal patterns and anomalies that matter for analysis. The project is built entirely on free, open NASA FIRMS data, so anyone can reproduce it.

It matters because responders, researchers and communities need one trusted picture of fire. A clear, consistent record lets them spot changes early and act sooner.
details:
What it does and how it works:
Fire Watch merges MODIS and VIIRS active-fire detections into a single dataset and shows it on a website. Both sensors are placed on a common grid. If both detect a fire in a cell we count it once, and if only one does we keep it. Fire intensity per cell is the larger of the two sensors’ totals, and each sensor’s confidence value is kept in its own column. Users get one combined map and an anomaly timeline (z-score analysis) showing seasonal trends and unusual events.

Benefits:
It removes double-counting, keeps early detections that only one sensor catches, and gives one consistent record that still shows trends, patterns and anomalies. No technical background is needed to use it.

Intended impact:
One trusted fire picture for responders, researchers and communities, so they can spot changes early and act sooner. Because it uses only free, open NASA data, it can be applied to any country.

Tools:
NASA FIRMS data (MODIS Aqua/Terra, VIIRS SNPP/NOAA-20).

Creativity:
Instead of choosing one satellite over the other, we treat them as partners that cover each other’s gaps. We judge the merge by whether the combined record still reveals trends, patterns and anomalies, and we made the result explorable by anyone, not just a dataset.

Factors considered:
Avoiding double-counting without losing real detections, different sensor resolution and timing, keeping each sensor’s confidence separate, validating that trends and anomalies survive the merge, and usability for non-experts.
